case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1)’s three criminal-history characteristics are conjunctive (disqualifying a defendant only if all three are present) or disjunctive (disqualifying if any one is present) for purposes of safety-valve relief from federal drug mandatory minimums.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1) (the First Step Act’s amended “safety valve” provision limiting applicability of statutory minimum sentences in certain federal drug cases).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pulsifer argues the statute’s use of the conjunction “and” means what it ordinarily means: a defendant fails § 3553(f)(1) (and is thus ineligible for safety-valve relief) only if he has (A) more than 4 criminal history points (excluding 1-point offenses) and (B) a prior 3-point offense and (C) a prior 2-point violent offense. Under this reading, having only one (or even two) of these characteristics does not bar safety-valve eligibility. He emphasizes textualism (ordinary meaning of “and”), argues the government’s alternative requires rewriting “and” to mean “or,” contends the Eighth Circuit’s reading creates unnecessary harshness inconsistent with the First Step Act’s expansion of safety-valve relief, and maintains that if any ambiguity remains, the rule of lenity requires adopting the more defendant-favorable (conjunctive) interpretation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues § 3553(f)(1) sets out three independent disqualifiers: a defendant is ineligible for safety-valve relief if he has more than four criminal-history points (as specified) or has a prior 3-point offense or has a prior 2-point violent offense. Although the statute uses “and,” the government contends the structure and function of the provision show Congress intended a disjunctive, eligibility-limiting list (i.e., any one condition triggers ineligibility). The government relies on contextual/structural canons to avoid readings it characterizes as anomalous or underinclusive (e.g., allowing defendants with serious criminal records to qualify) and argues that “and” can operate in a distributive way in negative eligibility criteria like this.
key_precedents: No specific Supreme Court merits precedents are identifiable from the excerpts provided; the dispute is presented primarily as a question of statutory text/grammar and interpretive canons (including the rule of lenity) and is described as a circuit conflict.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s Crooks v. Harrelson objection is the hardest point for the government because we should be wary of converting “and” to “or” in a criminal sentencing statute. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan explain, the clause is drafted as a negated eligibility screen—“does not have—(A)…; (B)…; and (C)….”—where ordinary usage is distributive, so each subparagraph operates as an independent disqualifier without judicially swapping conjunctions. Crooks cautions against redrafting, yet it does not control where the statute’s syntax, structure, and the function of § 3553(f) as multiple screens supply a best reading and avoid rendering (B) and (C) largely ineffectual for serious recidivists. For that same reason, I do not think Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s lenity arguments get traction: after applying text-in-context, any remaining uncertainty is not “grievous ambiguity.”

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s Crooks v. Harrelson point is the strongest textual objection, and I agree we must not “transmute” Congress’s conjunctions into disjunctions by judicial fiat. But, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, the clause is framed as a negated eligibility screen—“does not have—(A)…; (B)…; and (C)….”—where ordinary public meaning is distributive: the applicant must satisfy each listed criterion (i.e., lack each disqualifying trait), so the presence of any one defeats eligibility without rewriting “and” to “or.” Crooks therefore does not control because it addressed a different syntactic posture and did not purport to forbid context-sensitive distributive readings; here text, structure, and function resolve the meaning, leaving no “grievous ambiguity” for lenity, contrary to Justices Sotomayor and Jackson. I thus see no original-meaning basis to adopt petitioner’s conjunctive-only reading that would render (B) and (C) largely inert for the very class Congress was screening.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point is still Crooks v. Harrelson and the caution against effectively converting “and” to “or” in a criminal sentencing statute, but I do not think the distributive reading here requires that sort of judicial transmutation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the syntactic frame—“does not have—(A)…; (B)…; and (C)…”—is naturally read as requiring the defendant to lack each listed disqualifying trait, which preserves meaningful work for each subparagraph and fits § 3553(f)’s design as separate eligibility screens. I am also unpersuaded by Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s lenity arguments because, once text, syntax, and statutory role are applied, any remaining uncertainty is not the grievous ambiguity necessary to trigger lenity. Crooks remains a warning against rewriting, but in context this is ordinary English applied to a negated list, not a policy-driven substitution of conjunctions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I have considered Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s distributive-reading argument, but I still do not see a clear textual warrant to treat Congress’s repeated “and” across (A), (B), and (C) as three independent disqualifiers in a provision that governs mandatory-minimum exposure. Their underinclusiveness concern may be real as a matter of policy design, yet it cannot justify the kind of functional conjunction-to-disjunction move Crooks v. Harrelson cautions against, particularly where (B) and (C) still do meaningful work within the class already meeting (A), as Justice Gorsuch explains. Justice Barrett’s “negated eligibility screen” framing is linguistically possible, but the statute’s chosen syntax reasonably supports the conjunctive reading, and any remaining uncertainty should not be resolved to increase incarceration—lenity remains an appropriate backstop here. I therefore remain with the Petitioner.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is Crooks v. Harrelson’s warning that courts should not transmute “and” into “or,” especially in a sentencing statute; and Justice Sotomayor rightly adds that we should not fix perceived underinclusiveness by judicial revision. But here, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, we are not rewriting the conjunction—we are reading a negated eligibility formulation (“does not have—(A)…; (B)…; and (C)”) in its ordinary distributive sense, where the defendant must lack each listed disqualifier, so the presence of any one defeats relief without changing “and” to “or.” That text-in-context reading gives coherent operative effect to (B) and (C) within § 3553(f)’s screening structure, whereas the strictly conjunctive reading makes those subparts largely idle for many serious recidivists in a way that is hard to attribute to Congress’s drafting choice. Because that resolves meaning without “grievous ambiguity,” I agree with Roberts (and differ from Sotomayor/Jackson) that lenity does not properly enter under my methodology.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s distributive-reading argument is the strongest for Respondent: in a negated eligibility screen, ordinary speakers sometimes understand a listed series as separate disqualifiers. But here Congress did not write three freestanding screens; it wrote a single condition using a repeated, syntactically deliberate “and” across subparagraphs, and adopting Respondent’s view still functionally converts that integrated conjunctive into an “any-of” test in a way Crooks v. Harrelson warns against absent clearer textual signals. The asserted underinclusiveness and concerns about (B) and (C) doing less work under a conjunctive reading are, at bottom, policy inferences about what Congress must have intended—not the ordinary meaning of the words Congress enacted. And even if we end up with genuine residual uncertainty after the traditional tools, Justice Sotomayor’s point about mandatory-minimum exposure means lenity counsels against resolving that doubt to broaden punishment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s Crooks v. Harrelson warning is the strongest objection: we should not lightly transmute “and” into “or” in a criminal sentencing statute. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, this is not a substitution of conjunctions so much as applying ordinary, context-sensitive English to a negated eligibility screen (“does not have—(A)…; (B)…; and (C)…”) that naturally reads distributively—each listed characteristic is independently disqualifying. That reading also best fits § 3553(f)’s overall structure as multiple separate screening criteria (f)(1) alongside (f)(2)–(5), whereas petitioner’s conjunctive reading risks making (B) and (C) largely irrelevant for many defendants with serious records. Because the text-in-context yields a best reading, I agree with Roberts and Kagan that any remaining uncertainty is not the kind of “grievous ambiguity” that would trigger lenity, so I remain with Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s Crooks v. Harrelson point is the strongest objection: we must be wary of judicially transmuting “and” into “or,” particularly in a sentencing provision. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the statute’s negative, eligibility-screen syntax (“does not have—(A)…; (B)…; and (C)…”), read in ordinary English, operates distributively: the defendant must lack each listed disqualifying trait, so possessing any one defeats eligibility without rewriting the conjunction. That reading also avoids the functional nullification Justice Gorsuch downplays—under a strictly conjunctive approach, (B) and (C) frequently add no independent screening work for defendants already captured by (A), which is hard to square with § 3553(f)’s structure as multiple criteria. Because the text and structure resolve the meaning, I agree with the Chief that Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s lenity argument does not apply absent “grievous ambiguity.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s distributive-reading argument is the most serious for my position because it situates the phrase in a familiar “eligibility screen” structure and highlights the underinclusiveness that follows from a strictly conjunctive reading. But that underinclusiveness concern is ultimately a consequence-based critique of Congress’s drafting choice, and it does not, in my view, supply the clear textual warrant needed to treat “and” across (A), (B), and (C) as three independent disqualifiers—especially given Crooks v. Harrelson’s caution (pressed by Justice Gorsuch) against transmuting conjunctive text into a functional disjunction absent unequivocal contextual signals. Justice Barrett’s framing makes the respondent’s reading linguistically possible, yet the syntax remains genuinely contestable, and in a provision that determines exposure to mandatory minimums I do not think respondents have eliminated enough ambiguity to foreclose lenity, as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes. Under my pragmatic fairness lens, when Congress has not clearly chosen the harsher rule, we should not expand mandatory-minimum applicability by inference to “fix” perceived anomalies.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) is an eligibility-limiting provision keyed to criminal history, and in context it is most naturally read to exclude defendants who have any of the listed disqualifying characteristics (A), (B), or (C), rather than only the narrow subset who have all three at once. Reading the three subparagraphs conjunctively would create an underinclusive and anomalous scheme—allowing safety-valve relief for offenders with a serious 3-point prior or a 2-point violent prior so long as they lack one of the other traits—an outcome difficult to square with Congress’s use of criminal-history criteria as independent screens. Even if the text admits some syntactic uncertainty, the rule of lenity applies only after ordinary tools of statutory interpretation leave a clear, enduring ambiguity, and here the structure and function of § 3553(f) resolve the question without needing lenity. This narrower, context-based reading also best preserves uniform administration of federal sentencing and avoids judicial rewriting under the banner of expansionary purpose.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) denies safety-valve relief to a defendant who “does not have— (A) …; (B) …; and (C) …,” and in this eligibility-setting context the ordinary public meaning is distributive: the defendant must lack each listed characteristic, so possessing any one of (A), (B), or (C) defeats relief. Reading the “and” as requiring the Government to show all three disqualifiers would make the provision oddly underinclusive—allowing defendants with a serious prior 3-point offense or a 2-point violent offense to obtain relief so long as they lack one of the other characteristics—an atextual result inconsistent with the statute’s structure. The better textual reading treats the subparagraphs as three independent disqualifiers within a single negated condition, consistent with this Court’s attention to how a modifier and list operate in context. Because the text and structure supply the meaning, the rule of lenity does not apply here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) is an eligibility-limiting provision, and read in context its three subparagraphs operate as independent criminal-history disqualifiers: a defendant is ineligible if he has (A) more than four criminal-history points, (B) a prior 3-point offense, or (C) a prior 2-point violent offense. Although the word “and” typically conjoins, ordinary usage and statutory structure sometimes permit a distributive reading in negative, criteria-setting clauses to avoid making parts of the statute largely ineffectual and to prevent underinclusive results that would allow serious recidivists to evade mandatory minimums—an outcome difficult to reconcile with Congress’s calibrated expansion of relief in the First Step Act rather than a wholesale exemption. The canon against surplusage and practical-consequences considerations support treating each subparagraph as doing independent work, and any claimed ambiguity is not “grievous,” so the rule of lenity has no role. Textualism does not require an acontextual, hyperliteral reading when the statute’s design indicates Congress used “and” to link a list of separate disqualifying characteristics within § 3553(f)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) is written as a single eligibility bar defined by three subparagraphs joined by “and,” and reading it conjunctively best respects the ordinary meaning of Congress’s words while aligning with the First Step Act’s evident purpose to expand safety-valve relief for lower-level, nonviolent drug defendants. At minimum, the government’s disjunctive reading requires a context-driven grammatical move that creates substantial ambiguity about whether any one characteristic or only all three foreclose relief; that uncertainty in a penalty-setting provision should be resolved in favor of liberty. The rule of lenity applies to criminal penalty statutes, including sentencing provisions, and counsels against interpreting § 3553(f)(1) to broaden mandatory-minimum exposure absent clear congressional direction. See 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1); Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358, 410 (2010); Bifulco v. United States, 447 U.S. 381, 387 (1980).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) is best read in its full statutory context as setting out three independent criminal-history disqualifiers, even though the text uses “and,” because the provision functions as an eligibility screen and the ordinary grammar of coordinated criteria can operate distributively in such negative conditions. Reading it conjunctively (as requiring (A) and (B) and (C) all at once to bar relief) would make subsections (B) and (C) do little work for many offenders with serious records and would undermine the First Step Act’s calibrated expansion—broadening eligibility but still excluding offenders with specified serious priors—thus raising workability and coherence concerns. This contextual approach is consistent with the Court’s instruction that “and/or” are not mechanical and may yield to statutory structure and purpose when context demands. Because the text and structure supply a clear best reading, the rule of lenity does not apply here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) says the defendant is ineligible if he “has—(A) … and (B) … and (C) …,” and in ordinary English that conjunctive phrasing requires all three characteristics before the disqualification applies. Reading the “and”s to mean “or” would effectively revise Congress’s text, and the presumption of consistent usage is especially strong where Congress used “and” twice in the same sentence—once linking subsections (1)–(5) and again linking (A)–(C)—without any clear signal it intended different meanings. The government’s structural objections cannot justify departing from the enacted words; as Crooks v. Harrelson teaches, courts may override literal statutory terms only in truly extraordinary circumstances, and this case does not warrant that step. At minimum, if any genuine ambiguity remained in this criminal sentencing provision, the rule of lenity would require adopting the defendant-favorable conjunctive reading.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) is best read, in context, as setting out three independent criminal-history disqualifiers for safety-valve relief—consistent with the statute’s function as an eligibility screen for relief from otherwise-applicable mandatory minimums. Although “and” can be conjunctive, the Court has long recognized that in negative or distributive constructions the terms in a list may operate independently, and here a strictly conjunctive reading would create serious practical anomalies by allowing defendants with undeniably serious criminal histories (e.g., a prior 3-point offense) to qualify so long as they lack one of the other listed traits. Reading the provision disjunctively better fits the overall structure of § 3553(f), which requires satisfying multiple separate criteria for relief, and it avoids an interpretation that would be underinclusive in a way Congress is unlikely to have intended when amending the safety valve in the First Step Act. Because the text and structure resolve the question, the rule of lenity does not apply.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) denies safety-valve relief to a defendant who “does not have” the listed criminal-history traits, and in that negative-eligibility setting the best textual reading treats subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) as independent disqualifiers rather than a single cumulative package. Reading “and” strictly conjunctively would produce a counterintuitive scheme under which a defendant with a serious prior (a 3-point offense) or a violent prior (a 2-point violent offense) could still qualify so long as he lacks one of the other traits—an outcome difficult to square with the statute’s structure and the safety valve’s evident function. While Crooks v. Harrelson cautions that courts should not flip conjunctions absent “rare and exceptional circumstances,” 282 U.S. 55, 60 (1930), this interpretation does not rewrite the statute so much as apply “and” distributively to a list of separate ineligibility characteristics within § 3553(f)(1). Given that reading, lenity has no role because the text and structure resolve the question without grievous ambiguity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) is an eligibility-limiting exception to otherwise applicable mandatory minimum punishment, and Congress drafted the three disqualifying characteristics in a single sentence connected by the ordinary conjunctive “and,” which most naturally means a defendant is barred only if he has (A) and (B) and (C). At minimum, the government’s distributive reading creates substantial ambiguity when applied to a criminal sentencing statute that determines whether a mandatory minimum must be imposed, and that ambiguity should be resolved in the defendant’s favor under the rule of lenity after traditional interpretive tools do not decisively dispel it. See 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1); Abramski v. United States, 573 U.S. 169, 204 (2014) (Scalia, J., dissenting) (lenity applies when “all legitimate tools of interpretation ... do not decisively dispel the statute’s ambiguity”). This reading also better accords with the First Step Act’s practical aim of expanding safety-valve relief and avoids unnecessarily harsh mandatory minimums for low-level, nonviolent offenders who otherwise satisfy § 3553(f)’s procedural requirements.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the word "and" in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1) requires a defendant to lack all three listed criminal-history characteristics to qualify for safety-valve relief, or instead disqualifies a defendant who has any one of them.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1) (the federal drug "safety valve" limiting applicability of mandatory minimum sentences), as amended by the First Step Act
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pulsifer argues § 3553(f)(1) sets out three disqualifying criminal-history features connected by "and," so a defendant is ineligible for safety-valve relief only if he has all three: (A) more than 4 criminal history points (excluding 1-point offenses), (B) a prior 3-point offense, and (C) a prior 2-point violent offense. On this reading, having just one (or even two) of these characteristics does not automatically bar relief; the Eighth Circuit’s contrary interpretation effectively rewrites "and" to mean "or" (or uses a distributive/negative-proof reading to the same effect), and any lingering ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant’s favor under the rule of lenity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues § 3553(f)(1) uses "and" in a way that makes the three criteria independently disqualifying, so a defendant is ineligible for safety-valve relief if he has any one of the listed criminal-history characteristics (more than 4 points, or a prior 3-point offense, or a prior 2-point violent offense). The government contends this construction best fits the structure and purpose of the safety-valve provision and avoids implausible coverage that would follow from requiring all three conditions to be present before disqualification.
key_precedents: No specific Supreme Court merits precedents are identified in the provided excerpts; the materials primarily reflect statutory-text arguments (including discussion of the rule of lenity) and a circuit conflict rather than reliance on a particular controlling case.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s warning that we must not judicially convert Congress’s “and” into “or” in a criminal-sentencing statute is the most serious objection, and it fairly tees up lenity if genuine, persistent ambiguity remains. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas explain, the operative predicate is the prefatory negative (“does not have—”), which in ordinary drafting distributes across each listed item; that analysis gives independent force to each disqualifier without rewriting the conjunction. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s reliance on Moskal and Burrage does not change my view because those cases treat lenity as a last resort, and here the grammar-in-context and the provision’s gatekeeping role within an exception to mandatory minimums resolve the meaning without “grievous ambiguity.” I would keep the holding narrow—limited to this negated, prefatory-clause list structure—to protect institutional legitimacy and avoid suggesting any broader license to treat “and” as disjunctive.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest argument is that we must not judicially convert Congress’s “and” into “or,” especially in a sentencing statute, and that any remaining ambiguity should be resolved by lenity. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, the operative predicate is the prefatory negative (“does not have—”), which in ordinary English and legal drafting distributes across each listed item, so the defendant must lack A, lack B, and lack C; having any one means he “does have” at least one disqualifying characteristic, without rewriting the conjunction. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s reliance on Moskal and Burrage does not change my view because those cases make lenity a last resort after the full interpretive toolkit, and here the grammatical structure in context resolves the meaning without the sort of persistent, grievous ambiguity that would justify lenity. The petitioner’s reading also sits awkwardly with § 3553(f)(1)’s evident gatekeeping role within an exception to mandatory minimums, allowing serious criminal-history markers to be ignored so long as one other marker is absent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point remains that we should be wary of treating Congress’s “and” as if it were “or,” especially in a sentencing statute, and I agree that lenity can matter when genuine ambiguity persists. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, this text is not a free-standing “A, B, and C” list; it is a prefatory negative (“does not have—”) that, in ordinary drafting, distributes to each item, so eligibility requires lacking A, lacking B, and lacking C, meaning any one trait defeats the “does not have” condition without rewriting the conjunction. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s reliance on Moskal/Burrage does not change that, because those cases treat lenity as a last-resort tie-breaker only after ordinary grammatical and structural tools fail; here, grammar-in-context and § 3553(f)(1)’s gatekeeping role resolve the meaning. The petitioner’s conjunctive reading would also undercut that gatekeeping function by allowing defendants with plainly serious criminal-history markers (e.g., a 3-point prior) to qualify merely because they lack another marker, a consequence that confirms the ordinary reading rather than overrides it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point seriously that a prefatory negative can distribute across a series, and I agree that reading is grammatically available without literally substituting “or” for “and.” But in a criminal-sentencing gatekeeping provision, that structural intuition cannot do the work of overcoming Congress’s enacted conjunction where an equally ordinary reading is that disqualification requires all three listed traits; otherwise we effectively treat “and” as though it had disjunctive effect, expanding mandatory-minimum exposure without a clear textual command. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Barrett’s “implausible results” and surplusage arguments are not enough for me because overlap and underinclusive screens are common in criminal-history provisions, and perceived policy oddities cannot resolve genuine syntactic uncertainty. Under Moskal and Burrage—invoked by several colleagues—lenity remains a last resort, but here, after text, grammar, and structure are weighed, I still see persistent reasonable doubt, so lenity counsels against the harsher construction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest counterpoint: that a negated, conjunctive series can be read to require all listed traits and that we should hesitate—especially in sentencing—to deny eligibility absent clearer drafting. But, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the key grammatical move is not converting “and” to “or”; it is that the operative predicate “does not have” naturally distributes across the coordinated items in ordinary legal English, so any listed criminal-history marker makes the “does not have” statement false. That reading also coheres with § 3553(f) as a five-part eligibility checklist; petitioner’s construction makes (f)(1) an oddly weak gatekeeper by permitting serious criminal-history defendants to pass so long as one other marker is missing. Moskal and Burrage, invoked by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson, reinforce that lenity is a last-resort tiebreaker, and once grammar-in-context and statutory role resolve the negated list, we are not left with the kind of persistent, grievous ambiguity that triggers lenity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s point seriously that a prefatory negative (“does not have—”) often distributes across a series, and on many facts that yields a sensible screening rule. But that move does not eliminate the antecedent textual problem: Congress still chose a single negated clause followed by “and,” and ordinary English plausibly reads that construction to require the concurrence of all listed traits before the “does not have” condition is violated—especially in a sentencing statute where we should not infer broader mandatory-minimum exposure from an arguable syntactic implication. Justice Thomas’s surplusage/fit concerns and Justice Barrett’s “gatekeeping” intuition are policy-laden proxies for clarity; overlap and under-inclusiveness are common in criminal-history rules and do not supply the clear textual signal needed to treat “and” as functionally disjunctive. Moskal and Burrage, invoked by several colleagues, reinforce that lenity is a last resort, but if—after grammar, structure, and context—two reasonable readings persist and one increases punishment, lenity supplies the rule of decision rather than our sense of what Congress likely preferred.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that we must not rewrite “and” as “or” in a criminal-sentencing statute and should apply lenity if ambiguity persists—does not overcome the way the prefatory negative (“does not have—”) operates in ordinary legal drafting to distribute across each listed subparagraph, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain. On that reading, we do not transmute the conjunction; we apply the negation to each condition, so the defendant must lack A, lack B, and lack C to qualify, and having any one defeats the “does not have” requirement. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s invocation of Moskal/Burrage for lenity does not change my analysis because those cases treat lenity as a last-resort rule after the full interpretive toolkit, and here the syntax-in-context plus § 3553(f)(1)’s gatekeeping role resolves the meaning without grievous ambiguity. I also share Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional/workability concern that petitioner’s reading would produce a startling expansion of eligibility that sits awkwardly with Congress’s design of this subsection as a criminal-history screen within an exception to mandatory minimums.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that we must not treat Congress’s “and” as “or” in a criminal-sentencing statute and that any lingering uncertainty should trigger lenity, but that framing misdescribes what the respondent’s reading does. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, the operative predicate is the prefatory negative (“does not have—”), which in ordinary English and legal drafting distributes across a series, so the defendant must lack (A), lack (B), and lack (C) to qualify—meaning possession of any one defeats the “does not have” condition without rewriting the conjunction. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s reliance on Moskal and Burrage does not alter the analysis because those cases reserve lenity for persistent, grievous ambiguity after applying the full interpretive toolkit; here, the grammar-in-context and § 3553(f)’s checklist structure resolve the better reading. I therefore remain with the respondent because petitioner’s construction produces an implausible gatekeeping failure (e.g., permitting a serious 3-point prior to qualify) that an ordinary reader would not attribute to (f)(1).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s distribution point seriously, but I still do not see it as resolving the core syntactic choice: a negated series joined by “and” can be read either as three independent disqualifiers or as requiring the conjunction of all three listed traits before denial, and Congress did not draft this in the clearer “does not have (A) or (B) or (C)” form. Justice Barrett’s “gatekeeping” intuition and the “odd results” examples cannot substitute for textual clarity where the consequence is longer mandatory-minimum exposure; under Moskal and Burrage (as my colleagues invoke them), lenity remains available when ordinary tools leave persistent interpretive doubt, and here that doubt remains after grammar-in-context is applied. Justice Thomas’s surplusage argument also does not undermine my view because overlap among criminal-history criteria is common, and Congress can rationally choose cumulative screens without each subpart doing maximal independent work in every case. Given the remaining reasonable ambiguity in a sentencing-limiting statute, I would adhere to petitioner’s reading and apply lenity rather than treat “and” as effectively disjunctive through a contested distribution move.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) must be read in its full statutory context, and the better reading is that subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) are independent criminal-history disqualifiers—so a defendant who has any one of them fails § 3553(f)(1) and is ineligible for safety-valve relief. Although “and” ordinarily has conjunctive force, we have recognized that literalism can yield to context and evident design where a rigid reading would produce implausible results or defeat the provision’s operation; here, requiring a defendant to have all three serious criminal-history markers before disqualification would substantially expand eligibility in a way Congress is unlikely to have intended when tightening and tailoring mandatory-minimum relief. Because this interpretation resolves the statute on narrow textual-and-structural grounds and avoids creating a broad, counterintuitive eligibility rule, it best serves stable administration of the sentencing scheme and institutional legitimacy. The rule of lenity does not apply where, after considering text and context, the better reading is apparent and the statute is not grievously ambiguous.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text provides that safety-valve relief applies only if the defendant “does not have—(A) …; (B) …; and (C) …,” 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1); read in ordinary English, a negated list introduced by “does not have” describes the absence of each enumerated disqualifying trait, so possessing any one of (A), (B), or (C) defeats eligibility. Construing “and” to require all three traits for disqualification would stretch the statute from its evident function—limiting relief for offenders with serious criminal history—and would make (B) and (C) largely irrelevant for defendants who already exceed the points threshold, contrary to the ordinary expectation that each listed item does work. Context-sensitive application of the series-qualifier and related grammatical canons supports treating (A)–(C) as separate, independently disqualifying conditions tied to the single predicate “does not have,” and there is no grievous ambiguity triggering lenity. Our interpretive approach accords with the Court’s ordinary-meaning textualism in parsing list structure and modifiers.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1), read in context, uses “and” to link three independently disqualifying criminal-history characteristics, so a defendant is ineligible if he has any one of them; otherwise Congress would have created the odd result that a defendant with a serious prior (e.g., a 3-point offense) could still qualify so long as he lacks one of the other listed traits. That contextual, distributive reading best fits the safety-valve’s evident function—carving out only lower-history offenders from mandatory minimums—while avoiding a construction that would significantly expand eligibility in ways Congress likely did not intend. The rule of lenity does not apply because the statute’s structure and purpose resolve any uncertainty without leaving a grievous ambiguity. Nor is this an occasion to “override the literal terms” under the absurdity doctrine; rather, consistent with Crooks v. Harrelson, context can inform how “and” operates without rewriting the statute.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) is a remedial, access-to-justice provision designed to soften mandatory minimums, and its text uses the conjunctive “and” to link subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C), naturally indicating that relief is barred only when all three criminal-history features are present. At minimum, the competing readings show persistent ambiguity after ordinary tools of construction, and that uncertainty should not be resolved to narrow sentencing relief and expand mandatory-minimum exposure absent clear congressional command. Under the rule of lenity, where reasonable doubt remains about a criminal sentencing statute’s scope, courts must adopt the defendant-favorable interpretation rather than effectively rewriting “and” to mean “or.” See 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1); Moskal v. United States, 498 U.S. 103, 108 (1990); Burrage v. United States, 571 U.S. 204, 216 (2014).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3553(f) makes safety-valve relief available only if the court finds the defendant satisfies subsections (1) through (5), and in § 3553(f)(1) the prefatory negative (“does not have”) naturally distributes across each subpart, so a defendant must lack each of (A), (B), and (C) to qualify—meaning the presence of any one characteristic disqualifies. Reading “and” as requiring all three disqualifying traits simultaneously would create glaring workability problems and implausibly broaden eligibility to offenders with serious records (e.g., a prior 3-point offense) so long as they lack one of the other items, undermining the structure and evident gatekeeping function of (f)(1) after the First Step Act. The presumption of consistent usage yields to context, and here context supports the distributive reading of “and” in a negative list rather than the joint-satisfaction “and” used in § 3553(f)’s affirmative checklist. Because the text and statutory design resolve the question, lenity does not apply.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) says the court shall apply safety-valve relief if “the defendant does not have” characteristics (A), (B), and (C); in ordinary English, a negated list joined by “and” is naturally read conjunctively, requiring the government to show all three listed traits before disqualification. Reading “and” to mean “or” (or to operate distributively) is a substantial rewriting of the enacted text, and separation-of-powers principles counsel courts to apply Congress’s words as written rather than adjust them to better fit perceived policy aims. At minimum, the competing joint and distributive readings create genuine ambiguity in a provision that determines exposure to a mandatory minimum, triggering the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. Accordingly, Pulsifer remains eligible unless he possesses all three disqualifying criminal-history features in § 3553(f)(1)(A)–(C).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Reading § 3553(f)(1) in context, the most workable construction is that a defendant is ineligible for safety-valve relief if he has any one of the listed criminal-history characteristics, because § 3553(f) is an exception to otherwise-applicable mandatory minimums and Congress reasonably targeted recidivists through multiple independent disqualifiers. The petitioner’s all-three-required reading would create impractical and counterintuitive results—allowing relief for defendants with serious prior records (e.g., a prior 3-point offense) so long as they lack one of the other two features—undermining the statute’s evident function after the First Step Act amendment. Even if “and” can sometimes be read conjunctively, courts do not apply lenity unless, after considering text, structure, and purpose, a grievous ambiguity remains; here the structural fit and practical workability resolve the question against lenity. See 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1) (as amended); Maracich v. Spears, 570 U.S. 48, 76 (2013) (lenity only after full interpretive analysis leaves real ambiguity).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) says a defendant is eligible only if he “does not have—(A)…; (B)…; and (C)…,” and in ordinary legal drafting that negated list functions distributively: each listed criminal-history feature is independently disqualifying because the statute is describing a set of bars to relief. Reading “and” to require all three characteristics would create anomalous results—most notably, allowing safety-valve relief for defendants with a serious prior 3-point offense so long as they lack one of the other two traits—an implausible scheme given the safety valve’s role as a narrow exception to mandatory minimums. The broader structure (an eligibility carveout with multiple prerequisites in § 3553(f)(1)–(5)) and the need to read the provision coherently in context counsel against treating subsection (f)(1) as a “conjunctive negative proof” that would dramatically expand eligibility. Any residual uncertainty is not “grievous ambiguity” triggering lenity, because the statutory context and common usage resolve the choice in favor of the government’s reading.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3553(f)(1) sets eligibility by requiring the defendant to not have the listed characteristics, and Congress used the conjunctive “and” to join subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C); absent clearer textual signals, I would not effectively rewrite that conjunction into three independent disqualifiers. Given the safety valve’s remedial role in mitigating mandatory minimums after the First Step Act, the petitioner’s reading better aligns with practical consequences and proportional sentencing, especially for lower-level offenders. At minimum, after applying the traditional tools of construction, any remaining uncertainty about whether “and” operates conjunctively or distributively in this negative-eligibility provision should be resolved in the defendant’s favor under the rule of lenity. This Court has explained that lenity applies when, after ordinary interpretive tools, “reasonable doubt persists” about a criminal statute’s scope, Moskal v. United States, 498 U.S. 103, 108 (1990), and it cannot be displaced by an atextual demand for “grievous ambiguity.”
